title: Growing old (Psalm 71:9, 18)
hookLine: don't cast me off in old age; let me tell the next generation

lines: THE FEAR OF BEING SET ASIDE.
cards: Gray hair on the pillow. Reading glasses in three rooms of the house. A hand that shakes a little when it pours the coffee.

Somewhere in the Psalms is a prayer from someone who has noticed all of this in their own body, and is frightened. Not of dying, exactly. Of being set aside: the person nobody calls, whose stories nobody asks for anymore.
The psalm names that fear out loud, then does something unexpected with it. It asks for one more job.

teach.h: CAST ME NOT OFF IN OLD AGE.
teach.b: Psalm seventy-one, verse nine, in the King James words: "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth." That's the fear, plainly said.
The psalm doesn't pretend age is all wisdom and rocking chairs. Strength fails. People drift away.

teach.h: UNTIL I HAVE SHEWED THY STRENGTH.
teach.b: Later in the same psalm, the voice comes back with a request: "Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come."
Listen to the word until. Don't let me go until I've told them. This old person isn't asking to be kept comfortable, but useful.
They carry something the young don't have yet, a long memory of what God has done, and they want to hand it on.

teach.h: THE HOARY HEAD IS A CROWN.
teach.b: Proverbs says, "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness."

And in Luke's Gospel, when Mary and Joseph bring the baby Jesus to the temple, two people take the child to heart: Simeon, who had been told he would not see death before he saw the Lord's Christ, and Anna, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser, a widow Luke says was of a great age.
What does Anna do? She speaks of the child to everyone who looked for redemption in Jerusalem. She tells the next generation.
The psalm's picture is simple: the old are not finished. They carry the stories across.

how: Christians pray for and visit older members of their churches, take communion to people who can no longer come, and in some congregations grandparents and elders pass on the faith by teaching, telling their stories and praying with the young.

o: a time the Bible says to spend resting from all your labors
a fear named honestly, and a calling to pass on what God has done
a season for stepping back quietly and letting the young lead

p: until I have shewed thy strength
the job the psalm asks for
a crown of glory, in Proverbs
spoke of the child to all who waited

s: Psalm 71 pretends that old age is easy
it says it plainly: forsake me not when my strength faileth.
the psalm asks to be kept until it has told the next generation
"until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation."
in Luke, only young people greet the baby Jesus in the temple
Anna, a widow of a great age, gives thanks and speaks of him to everyone waiting.

games.q: you're Anna, old and widowed, in the temple when a young couple brings in their baby. you know who this child is. what do you do?
o: keep it to yourself; you're too old to be listened to.
give thanks, and tell everyone who is waiting.
go home and rest; someone younger will tell them.
games.why: Luke says she gave thanks and spoke of him to all who looked for redemption in Jerusalem. the old widow in the scene is the one who spreads the news.

practice: Bring to mind someone older than you, a grandparent, a neighbor, someone from church or work, and picture their face.
Find one question you've never asked them, what was your hardest year, who taught you to pray, or not to, what do you want us to remember, and simply hold it.
If you pray, you can pray the psalm's own words for them: cast them not off.

wordCard.voice: Growing old. In Psalm seventy-one, it's a fear named honestly, and a calling: to show God's strength to the generation that comes next.

orig.note: Hebrew: gray hair, old age — the word in Psalm 71:18 for the gray head of the one praying.

carryVoice: Your line: tell the next generation. In this psalm, gray hair still has work to do. See you tomorrow.
